title: Machine Learning
overview: Machine Learning is AI that learns rules from examples instead of being told the rules directly.

sections.label: What is Machine Learning & Supervised Learning

blocks.title: What is What is Machine Learning & Supervised Learning?
blocks.body: Machine Learning is AI that learns rules from examples instead of being told the rules directly.
bullets: Machine Learning: data + correct answers = rules (AI figures out the rules itself)
Supervised Learning: training with labeled examples — input + correct output given
Classification: predict a category (spam or not spam, pass or fail)
Regression: predict a number (house price, student score)

analogy.title: Think of ML as Learning to Sort Laundry

blocks.instructions: Classify each problem as classification or regression.

blocks.expectedOutput:

blocks.title: What is Unsupervised & Reinforcement Learning?
blocks.body: Not all learning needs labels. Unsupervised learning finds patterns on its own. Reinforcement learning learns by trying and getting rewards.
bullets: Unsupervised Learning: finds patterns with no labels — grouping similar customers
Clustering: grouping similar data points together automatically
Reinforcement Learning: AI tries an action, gets a reward or penalty, learns over time
Example: chess AI learns by playing millions of games — rewarded for winning
Overfitting: model memorizes training data but fails on new data

analogy.title: Think of Reinforcement Learning as Training a Puppy
analogy.description: Learn by trial and error with rewards

blocks.title: Identifying Learning Paradigms
blocks.instructions: Match each scenario to the correct learning paradigm: supervised, unsupervised, or reinforcement.
blocks.hint: Supervised uses labeled data, Unsupervised finds patterns, Reinforcement uses rewards.
blocks.expectedOutput:
Chess AI learns by playing games: reinforcement
Grouping customers by purchase patterns: unsupervised
Email spam detector trained on labeled emails: supervised

blocks.title: What is ML Steps?
bullets: Step 1: Collect data — gather examples of inputs and correct outputs
Step 2: Clean data — remove errors, fill missing values
Step 3: Train model — feed data to algorithm, it learns the pattern
Step 4: Test model — give it new unseen data, check accuracy
Step 5: Predict — use trained model on real-world inputs

analogy.title: Think of ML Pipeline as a Factory Assembly Line
analogy.description: Raw data goes through stages to produce predictions

blocks.title: Simple Linear Regression
blocks.code:
# Simple linear regression: y = mx + b
# Training data: hours studied vs exam score
hours = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
scores = [50, 55, 65, 70, 75]

# Calculate slope (m) and intercept (b)
n = len(hours)
m = (n * sum(h*s for h,s in zip(hours, scores)) - sum(hours)*sum(scores)) / (n*sum(h*h for h in hours) - sum(hours)**2)
b = (sum(scores) - m * sum(hours)) / n

print(f"Formula: score = {m:.1f} * hours + {b:.1f}")
print(f"Predicted score for 6 hours: {m*6+b:.0f}")
blocks.expectedOutput:
Formula: score = 6.5 * hours + 44.0
Predicted score for 6 hours: 83

keyTakeaways.text: ML learns rules from data instead of being told rules directly
Supervised learning uses labeled data — input + correct output
Classification predicts categories; Regression predicts numbers
Unsupervised learning finds patterns with no labels
Reinforcement learning learns through rewards and penalties
Overfitting is when a model memorizes data instead of learning the pattern
